---
title: "What it does"
description: >-
  Every shortcut, what each one previews, and how the contact sheet, the EPUB conversion and the annotations work from a reader's side.
---

## Shortcuts

Every action has exactly one shortcut, and every one of them is
[configurable](settings.qmd).

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Space** | Preview the selected item's attachment. Again, or **Escape**, to dismiss. |
| **Shift+Space** | Preview the item's notes, rendered as a page. |
| **Ctrl+Shift+Space** | Contact sheet: every page of a PDF as a thumbnail, or a book’s printed pages. |
| **Ctrl+Alt+Space** | The same sheet in a Zotero window: it scrolls under the keyboard and needs no system preview. Again to close it — or **Escape**, **Space** or **q**, the keys that close the system preview. A click on a page hands over to the reader and closes it. |

Each shortcut is its own switch: the press that put a preview up takes it down
again, and **Escape** does the same. A different shortcut while one is showing
switches to what it shows — a contact sheet gives way to the plain preview of
the same file on Space, and back on the sheet's shortcut.

On Linux that holds while Zotero has the keyboard. GNOME focuses the preview as
it opens — the same happens when Files opens one — and from then on the window
answers its own keys: **Space**, **Escape** or **q** close it, and the **arrow
keys** walk your item list with the preview following, exactly as they walk the
file list in Files. Back in Zotero, the shortcuts speak again.

The same actions sit in the right-click menu. The contact sheet entries appear
only when the selection actually contains a PDF or an EPUB.

The defaults are the same on every system; only the way they are written
differs, since ⌃⇧ are macOS keycaps and mean nothing elsewhere. They avoid the
combinations the systems take for themselves — Spotlight, input-source
switching, and the window menu a window manager claims before the application
is ever asked. There is more on that in [Architecture](dev/architecture.qmd).

Space is ignored while the item list is collecting a find-as-you-type search, so
typing a title with spaces in it still searches.

## What it previews

Anything the system's preview panel can show: PDFs, images, video, HTML, plain
text, office documents, and whatever a third-party preview extension adds. The
plugin hands the file over untouched.

**EPUB is the exception.** No system preview renders one, so zotLook converts
the book on the fly into a single styled page: the spine walked in reading
order, each chapter's body appended, the book's own stylesheets pulled in so its
layout and typography survive, and a Palatino base font in a book-width column
laid over the top. Images, fonts and inline SVGs resolve, because relative URLs
in both markup and CSS are rewritten. A converted book is cached until the file
changes.

**Your annotations are in it.** Zotero stores the position of an EPUB
annotation as an EPUB CFI — spine item, element path, character offsets — and
zotLook resolves that identifier against the chapter it names, so a passage is
marked where you marked it. Highlights carry their colour at half opacity and
underlines are drawn as underlines, the way Zotero's own reader draws them, and
palettes beyond Zotero's eight work as well as its own.

**A button in each corner** opens the contents and the annotations over the
page. The contents come from the navigation the book carries, so the titles and
their nesting are the publisher's rather than guesses drawn from headings; the
annotations are listed in reading order, each quotation cut to two lines until
you unfold it, and clicking one takes you to the passage. Both are `<details>`
and CSS — a preview panel runs no scripts, so a menu needing one would never
open. A book with no navigation gets no contents button.

Because the plugin cannot reliably tell whether you have an EPUB preview
extension installed, the conversion is a [setting](settings.qmd) rather than a
guess: turn it off and the book goes to the panel like any other file.

## The contact sheet

Every page of a PDF as a thumbnail in a scrollable grid — useful for finding the
figure you remember, or for seeing at a glance which pages you marked up.

- **Annotations are drawn in**, so the marked-up pages stand out.
- **A button in each corner** opens the document's own contents and its
  annotations over the grid, as the EPUB preview has them: the contents from
  the PDF's outline, the annotations in reading order with the quotation, the
  comment and the page. Clicking an entry brings that page to the middle of
  the window, framed. A PDF without an outline gets no contents button, and
  both buttons can be switched off.
- **Clicking a page opens it in Zotero's reader** at that page. This works from
  the preview panel on macOS and Windows, and from the window variant
  everywhere — Sushi's view cannot follow a `zotero:` link, which is what the
  window variant is for on Linux.
- **The layout adapts.** A document with few pages gets fewer columns and
  correspondingly sharper thumbnails, so it fills the width instead of leaving
  space. The column count is configurable.
- **No page limit by default.** A 300-page book takes a few seconds. A limit can
  be set for unusually large scans; when it bites, the sheet says how many pages
  it is showing.

The window variant (**Ctrl+Alt+Space**) puts the same sheet in a Zotero window,
where it scrolls under the keyboard and needs no system preview. A click hands
over the same way everywhere: the reader opens at that page, and sheet and
panel alike close behind the handoff.

**The window can search.** A field in its top corner, also reached with
Ctrl+F, takes a word or a phrase: pages without it are dimmed, pages with it
show how often, the first is brought to the middle, and Enter walks on to the
next. The text comes off the pages as the sheet is drawn, so a scan without a
text layer has nothing to search. The system previews have no field, since
they run no scripts; the sheet there is the same, minus the search.

**The window answers the keyboard.** The frame is a cursor:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| **Enter** | frames the next page — the first, on the first press — or, with a search, the next hit; **Shift+Enter** goes back |
| **Arrow keys** | move the frame across the grid, a row at a time up and down; with a search, between the hits |
| **o**, or **Ctrl+Enter** | opens the framed page in the reader, as a click does, and the window closes behind it |
| **c** / **a** | open the contents or the annotations; the arrows walk the entries, **Enter** or **o** follows one, the same letter closes the menu |
| **Page Up** / **Page Down** | scroll, as before |
| **Space**, **q**, **Escape** | close the window |

In the search field a letter is typing, and the left and right arrows move
the caret; Enter and the up and down arrows work there as they do outside it.

### A page overview of a book

The same shortcut on an EPUB gives a sheet too — which sounds impossible,
because a reflowable book has no pages. It has none of its own. But a book
published beside a print edition usually carries that edition's pagination
along with it, marked in the text and listed in the navigation, so that a
citation to page 212 still means something. Where those marks are there, zotLook
cuts the book at them and shows a page at a time.

- **Each tile is that page's own text**, in the book's own typography, shrunk.
  It is not a facsimile — the printed layout is in the PDF and nowhere in the
  EPUB — but it is enough to see where a table sits or a chapter begins.
- **Clicking a page opens the book at it**, in Zotero's reader, exactly as the
  PDF sheet's thumbnails do — at the very position the reader keeps for that
  page. In paginated flow the reader shows whole columns and names the page at
  a column's top, so a page whose mark falls partway down a column is shown
  within the column above it; scrolled flow lands on it exactly. Zotero's own
  page navigation behaves the same way.
- **Annotations are drawn in**, as they are on the PDF sheet and in the EPUB
  preview.
- **The same two buttons** as on the PDF sheet: the book's navigation and its
  annotations, each entry a jump to the page's tile.
- **The same search** in the window variant, and here the hits are marked
  in the tiles themselves, since a tile is the page's own text. The keys are
  the same as well.
- **A book without printed page numbers says so.** Most trade fiction carries
  none, and nothing can invent one; a sheet of arbitrary slices would be worse
  than none. Academic publishers — Springer, O'Reilly, most textbooks — usually
  do carry them.

## Which attachment gets previewed

Selecting a parent item previews **one** of its attachments. By default the
order is PDF, EPUB, HTML, image, video, anything else — and it is a ranking, not
a filter: a type near the bottom is still used when nothing above it is present.
You can [reorder it](settings.qmd), or switch to simply taking the first
attachment the item lists.

Only the chosen attachment is ever resolved. Resolving them all would download
every synced attachment of every selected item only to throw all but one away.

## Localisation

Menu entries, settings and progress messages are available in English and
German, following Zotero's own language setting.
